analysis.title: Top of Mind Issue 153: Is the AI investment cycle durable?
key_insights: Recent AI-related stresses in equity and credit markets, circular financing arrangements and new regulatory uncertainty after the US midterms are raising questions about how long the current pace of AI spending can continue. GS interviews Chamath Palihapitiya (Social Capital), Eric Sheridan, Miriam Wheeler, Gabriela Borges, Amanda Lynam and Ryan Hammond.

Palihapitiya says there is a mismatch between promised data center capacity, actual capacity and returns. Neoclouds make large commitments for GPUs, power and data centers, while the demand supporting them depends on end-customers earning a return on AI spending.

Palihapitiya says the number of companies that can attribute earnings or profitability gains to AI is essentially zero today. Change management, employee pushback and productivity gains lost elsewhere in the value chain slow diffusion.

Palihapitiya describes neoclouds as using speculative short-term revenue to support long-dated fixed obligations, with a business that depends on utilization. He puts neocloud break-even utilization at roughly 70-75%, against 80-85% for airlines. If token demand stays in the experimentation bucket, neoclouds sit in a 75-85% utilization zone where they make money but not enough to repay debt before hardware is obsolete.

Palihapitiya says chip and model efficiency gains may improve AI economics for customers but not for neoclouds, which must amortize long-dated GPU purchases. Demand has to grow enough to offset those efficiency gains.

Palihapitiya says SPVs financing the data center buildout are well isolated, but most sit under an investment-grade wrapper, so the risk traces back to hyperscalers. He expects hyperscalers to withstand a slowdown and to absorb the assets of failing neoclouds. Neoclouds that own land, power and shell are better placed than those that lease.

Palihapitiya expects a rationalization with asset redistribution rather than a 1999-style crash. In a stress case the weakest credits could face borrowing costs near 20%, CDS spreads could approach 1000bp and even IG borrowers could face near-double-digit funding costs. He calls the next 18 months critical for a clearing process.

Borges says CoreWeave's true cost of debt is lower than many investors assume. Its secured DDTLs, the primary financing source, price well below the 16% yield-to-worst on its $10bn of unsecured debt. She sees a very low probability of further pressure on its debt service because contracts are take-or-pay, debt is drawn only when data centers are ready, and debt self-amortizes within the contract life.

Borges attributes part of the rise in CoreWeave's CDS to investors hedging infrastructure exposure, since it is one of the few liquid data center CDS instruments. GS base case has CoreWeave capex reaching steady state in 2028 and free cash flow turning positive in 2030. CoreWeave revenue is on track to grow 150%+ in 2026, and 95%+ of its business is 4-5 year take-or-pay contracts.

Borges estimates another $500bn of IG issuance from hyperscalers could be supported, benchmarked against US banks. Non-IG financing needs may be smaller than expected given BYO-hardware, vendor prepayments, the $19tn private markets universe ($4.5tn to be put to work per Preqin) and Nvidia's $500bn financing pool.

GS sees the key demand test as hyperscalers needing $1.42tn of cumulative revenue over 2028-2030, roughly $500bn per year, to earn a 15% ROIC on 2026-2027E capex. The supply risk is a large amount of capacity coming online over the next two years, which could cut compute prices, especially for neoclouds selling on the spot market.

Wheeler says AI high yield supply has contracted sharply, with no new deals in the last month. About 30 AI deals came over the prior 12 months, and the market had been expecting $60bn of issuance this fall. She expects the market to bifurcate, favoring experienced developers with permits, IG wrappers and manageable size, and says data center deals can still get done.

Wheeler says high yield data center risk centers on non-IG tenants and on IG-wrapped leases where the wrapper only takes effect on completion. Developers typically have a 180-day late-delivery grace period before the tenant can terminate. Bonds often mature in 5 years against 15-20 year leases, creating refinancing risk.

Wheeler says GPU-backed facilities typically have a 3-5 year weighted average life and fully amortize. Chips are about 75% of data center cost against about 25% for shell and power, so the volume of hardware needing financing could pressure spreads. She is not particularly concerned about systemic contagion.

Wheeler is watching Texas, where the Governor-Elect has discussed a data center moratorium, hyperscaler debt trading levels and stabilization of volatility in existing names. She says high yield borrowing costs are effectively priced as a derivative of where hyperscalers trade, and that shelved projects permanently remove capacity from the pipeline.

Lynam says market saturation is the most binding constraint on AI debt issuance. Hyperscalers have issued $296bn of debt YTD, including $67bn+ announced since October 29, above GS's $250bn full-year forecast. GS estimates $687bn of global AI-related debt issuance YTD, with 43% from hyperscalers.

Lynam tracks $1.7tn of hyperscaler lease commitments, 75% not yet commenced, and $1.9tn of other unconditional purchase commitments, $685bn of which is due by year-end 2027. Hyperscaler free cash flow has turned negative.

Rating agencies are more cautious. Moody's said hyperscaler commitments are up eight-fold since 2023 (Sept 22), and S&P (Oct 15) said the margin for error is narrowing. S&P recently lowered the rating outlooks of Broadcom and Meta citing off-balance sheet obligations. Lynam says evidence of monetization by 2028 is key to limiting ratings pressure.

Sheridan sees the concerns as understandable rather than warranted or overblown, and says this is the third AI drawdown in 12-18 months (last fall/winter, this summer, now), each tied to return visibility 18-24 months out. He says this time is not different, though stakes are higher.

Sheridan says AWS, Azure and Google Cloud reported a combined revenue backlog of $1.8tn as of 3Q26, up about 140% y/y. Some hyperscalers expect roughly 50% of backlogs to convert to revenue over two years. He estimates the six hyperscalers can easily achieve a 15%+ ROIC, implying about $1.42tn cumulative revenue over 2028-30 without converting existing backlog, and assumes no further backlog growth.

Sheridan cites Q3 results: Alphabet ROIC well above its WACC, Amazon guiding to 40%+ growth for two years, and Meta reporting mid-20% growth against the 12% he expected a year ago. He expects agentic AI to raise token consumption just under 25x over five years, with frontier tokens keeping value and routine tokens commoditizing.

Sheridan says circular financing worries him, comparing it to late-1990s telecom, but he sees it concentrated in the supply chain rather than at Meta, Amazon and Alphabet. He says an unwind would come from disappointing demand, lack of access to capital or lack of power. Microsoft's debt raise was 5x oversubscribed weeks after CoreWeave's debt stress. He names hyperinflation in memory pricing and higher input costs as negative developments.

Sheridan says regulation making data centers harder to build would first slow supply rather than demand and could support the economics of existing assets. Greater risk sits with ecosystem participants whose revenue is concentrated in AI and who trade at single- to low-double-digit EPS multiples. Regulation that constrains how AI is deployed or monetized would hit demand.

Hammond says the six hyperscalers (Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, SpaceX) are on track for $890bn of capex in 2026, with FactSet consensus implying a further $1.4tn next year. GS analysts estimate about $350bn of annual AI revenue is needed to break even, and the application layer would need over $1tn annually at a 20% EBIT margin and 20% hyperscaler ROIC.

Hammond says corporate AI adoption is early. In Q3 earnings season about half of S&P 500 firms discussed internal AI use cases, 13% quantified productivity impact on a use case and 4% quantified earnings impact. Some token volume measures slowed in summer but have rebounded. Corporates spend about $1.5tn a year on software that could be reallocated, and GS economists estimate $1.8tn of potential annual US labor productivity gains.

Interviewees agree investors should position for safety: Wheeler sees a continued move up in credit quality, and Palihapitiya and Sheridan see hyperscalers as relatively well positioned thanks to strong balance sheets, diversified businesses and existing capacity.

Macro snapshot: GS expects the next 25bp Fed hike in December 2026, a final 25bp ECB hike in December, a second BoE hike in Feb 2027, and pulled forward its BoJ hike to December from January 2027. It cut its 2027 Euro area growth forecast to 0.9% from 1.3%, raised Euro area peak core inflation to 2.9% in 2Q27, and raised 2026 China GDP growth to 4.6% from 4.5%. Democrats won larger-than-expected House and Senate majorities in the midterms.

market_movers.rationale: Borges argues CoreWeave's true cost of debt is lower than assumed and sees very low probability of further pressure on debt service. Its CDS and bond yields have risen, with $10bn of unsecured debt at a 16% yield-to-worst.
Sheridan notes Microsoft's debt raise was 5x oversubscribed the week after CoreWeave's debt stress, showing hyperscaler financing access.
S&P recently lowered Meta's rating outlook citing off-balance sheet obligations. Sheridan separately cites mid-20% revenue growth in Q3.
S&P recently lowered Broadcom's rating outlook citing off-balance sheet obligations among the factors.

sector_views.rationale: Neoclouds depend on utilization and end-customer ROI, with those owning land, power and shell better placed than lessees. Borges sees CoreWeave's financing risk as low, while Palihapitiya sees a business with little margin for error.

Sheridan estimates a 15%+ ROIC, and Sheridan and Palihapitiya both cite strong balance sheets, cash flows and existing capacity. Lynam flags saturation of IG issuance and off-balance sheet obligations.
Supply has stalled, spreads widened, and Wheeler expects bifurcation with investors moving up in credit quality.

crypto_views: CoreWeave pivoted from using GPUs for bitcoin mining to compute services, per the GS neocloud Q&A.
risk_factors: Demand shortfall: end-customers fail to earn ROI on AI spending, leaving neocloud utilization too low to service debt.
Access to capital: market saturation from IG issuance and off-balance sheet obligations, rating pressure and higher costs for non-IG issuers.
Power: energy cannot scale as fast as land and shell, so the ecosystem could be short of power.
Supply overbuild: capacity coming online over the next two years could cut compute prices, mainly hurting spot-market neoclouds.
Circular financing in the supply chain, compared by Sheridan to the late-1990s telecom buildout.
Regulation and local politics, including a possible Texas data center moratorium, could slow supply or constrain AI deployment and monetization.
Refinancing risk on high yield data center bonds that mature in about 5 years against 15-20 year leases.
Late project delivery beyond the 180-day grace period can let tenants terminate leases and void IG wrappers.
Token price deflation and open-source models such as DeepSeek could limit hyperscaler monetization.
Memory price inflation and higher input costs raise the cost of the buildout.

Chart on p.15 shows AI buildout infrastructure spending as a share of GDP against canals, railroads, electrification, highways and telecom, with text stating it is on track to reach a larger share of GDP than any previous technology investment cycle.
Table on p.14 sizes required application layer revenue by hyperscaler ROIC and application layer EBIT margin, with text stating over $1tn annually at 20% EBIT margin and 20% ROIC.
vol_and_positioning: CoreWeave 5y CDS spreads have widened sharply and its CRWV 9 3/4 2031 bond yield has risen, which Borges attributes partly to investors using it as a liquid hedge for data center infrastructure exposure.
CDS spreads have drifted up among hyperscalers (Meta, Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Oracle).
AI-related spreads have widened in both USD high yield and USD investment grade, most in high yield.
AI stocks have sold off in recent months while the S&P 500 ex-AI has risen. Infrastructure stocks fell the most, with hyperscalers following more recently.
In a stress case, Palihapitiya says the weakest credits could face borrowing costs near 20% and CDS spreads near 1000bp.
geopolitical: Democrats won much larger-than-expected House and Senate majorities in the US midterms, which GS expects them to use at fiscal deadlines to seek concessions on the Iran war, tariffs and spending cuts.
Texas Governor-Elect has discussed a data center moratorium, a local policy risk for AI data center financing.
Higher energy prices from the Iran war weigh on the Euro area growth outlook and lift inflation forecasts.
Japan's Prime Minister Takaichi announced a phased reduction of measures curbing higher fuel prices.
cross_bank_references: GS US senior portfolio strategist Ryan Hammond sees an even higher revenue wall for the application layer than for the hyperscalers, but argues it is also potentially achievable.
Moody's highlighted that hyperscaler aggregate financial commitments have increased eight-fold since 2023.
S&P noted it sees the margin for error narrowing in the AI funding ecosystem, and lowered rating outlooks for Broadcom and Meta.

tension_points.bull_case: Sheridan estimates the six hyperscalers can easily earn a 15%+ ROIC, backlogs are $1.8tn (up about 140% y/y), and demand is gaining momentum with supply far from matching it. GS expects enterprise adoption to broaden.
tension_points.bear_case: Palihapitiya says the number of companies attributing earnings gains to AI is essentially zero, and capex is rising faster than visible ROI. Only 4% of S&P 500 firms quantified an earnings impact, and hyperscaler capex now exceeds operating cash flow.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Demand disappointing, lack of access to capital, or lack of power would turn the trough of disillusionment into a more permanent contraction.

tension_points.bull_case: Borges says secured DDTLs price well below the 16% unsecured yield, contracts are 95%+ take-or-pay, and the debt self-amortizes. CDS widening is partly hedging demand.
tension_points.bear_case: Palihapitiya says neoclouds fund long-dated fixed obligations with speculative short-term revenue and a small utilization cushion, with nothing needing to get much worse for the bear case to play out.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Too much compute supply arriving over the next two years, cutting prices, or utilization settling in the 75-85% gray zone, would hurt neocloud returns.

tension_points.bull_case: GS estimates another $500bn of IG issuance can be absorbed, and Microsoft's debt raise was 5x oversubscribed. Non-IG financing needs may be smaller than expected.
tension_points.bear_case: Lynam says market saturation is the binding constraint, with hyperscaler issuance of $296bn above forecast, $1.7tn of leases and $1.9tn of purchase commitments, and rating agencies turning cautious.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence of monetization by 2028 is the signpost for easing rating pressure. Failing that, S&P-style outlook cuts spreading across the AI ecosystem would worsen funding conditions.
